instructions:
## The project being researched

An XGBoost "virtual sensor" for Iowa stream nitrate: predict at locations with NO physical sensor, using only weather + land-use data. Two targets:
- REGRESSION: daily-max nitrate concentration (mg/L)
- CLASSIFICATION (the primary one): binary `violation` = daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263

~85 sensor sites, 160,074 site-days, 2008-2026. Each site has a delineated upstream drainage basin. Features are aggregated over basin cells in distance buckets from the outlet.

## THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET - judge every recommendation against this
The shipped product takes an ARBITRARY MAP PIN anywhere in Iowa, delineates its upstream basin on the fly via USGS NLDI, builds features from weather and land use alone, and predicts daily violation probability. There is NO nitrate history at the target location, NO discharge gauge there, and NO guarantee of a monitored neighbor upstream. Any method that requires the target site's own observations, or requires a gauged upstream site, DOES NOT WORK for this product - it may still be useful for other purposes, but that limitation must be stated explicitly and prominently.

## Current honest performance (leave-one-basin-family-out, LOFO)
- CLF: AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift over base rate), recall 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate, MCC 0.466, Brier 0.137
- REG: R2 0.328, RMSE 4.36 mg/L
- Deployed at beta=2: recall 0.864, but 59% of alarms are false

## THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the model cannot rank sites
- within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21
- macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24
The project's own summary: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." It captures WHEN nitrate rises at a given site, but fails at the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an unseen basin. Essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term.

## CRITICAL SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT
The ~85 sites collapse to only 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES under the leak-safe CV (sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time are grouped). So learning a site's absolute level is a regression with roughly 19 effective independent units, NOT 160k rows. Any method whose published gains come from hundreds of catchments (e.g. CAMELS with 531-671 basins) must be explicitly flagged as possibly infeasible here.

## Current features (68 for CLF)
9 weather variables x 3 distance buckets (SAME-DAY SCALARS ONLY), 8 CDL crop classes x 3 buckets, 2 nitrogen-surplus x 3 buckets, doy_sin/doy_cos, 4 cross-site nitrate lags (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), 5 static (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor).
Top features by permutation importance: rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, lon, lat, doy_sin, fuel_moisture_1000h. BOTTOM: all daily weather; precip_in_1d is dead last (perm ~0.000).

## KNOWN NEGATIVE RESULTS - do not naively re-propose these
- Lagged weather copies: HURT badly (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019)
- Rolling precip / water balance as implemented: worse (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003)
- Broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time: much worse (-0.166)
- Rolling (3D/7D) smoothed targets: worse
- Spike / anomaly z-score targets: failed cross-site (lofo_r2 ~ -0.0006)
- Antecedent moisture + rain x surplus interactions: REG a wash, CLF only +0.017 PR-AUC
- Riparian 0-2km bucket: CLF +0.039 PR-AUC but REG worse
- Advective travel-time routing IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and is part of the "lagged weather hurt" failure.
PATTERN: nearly every hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL feature has failed. The only wins came from geometry and static geography. This strongly suggests the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE static information, not in temporal dynamics.

## Data present on disk but UNUSED
- discharge/streamflow: only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS, 0.66-0.97 density, up to 18 years). ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites.
- co-located water chemistry: specific conductance (65 sites), water temp (80), pH (64), dissolved oxygen (64), turbidity + phosphate (61)
- upstream_uid (28 sites) / downstream_uid (40 sites) river-network topology: completely unread
- draining_area (80/85), NHDPlus comid (stored per basin), basin containment graph (used only to build CV folds)

## Known data problems
- Nitrogen surplus (gTREND product) ENDS IN 2017 -> NaN for 68% of training rows
- 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data; an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest multi-state basins)
- Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet


## Non-negotiable rules for this research

1. RECORD THE SPLIT PROTOCOL FOR EVERY PERFORMANCE NUMBER, AND DO NOT COMPARE NUMBERS ACROSS PROTOCOLS. Random-split results are valid evidence about method behavior and should be reported - researchers using them often have good reasons for their own question. But only SPATIALLY HELD-OUT numbers (leave-one-basin-out, leave-one-region-out, ungauged-basin protocol) are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, because a random split over autocorrelated site-days lets a model memorize a site's level and measures interpolation rather than transfer. When the protocol cannot be determined, say so rather than guessing.
2. REPORT EFFECT SIZES AND SAMPLE SIZES, NOT CONCLUSIONS. "GNNs improve water quality prediction" is worthless. "Recurrent GCN, 456 reaches, 42 monitored, held-out-node RMSE 1.83 vs 2.11 for LSTM" is actionable. Always give the number of catchments/basins/sites used.
3. EVERY DATASET RECOMMENDATION MUST BE OPERATIONAL: exact name, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage years, whether it covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins, exact URL, access mechanism (API/bulk/FTP), authentication requirement, and license.
4. ACTIVELY HUNT FOR NEGATIVE RESULTS. Seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed on this project. Papers reporting that a technique did NOT transfer are as valuable as successes and are systematically under-published - look in discussion/limitations sections and in benchmark comparison papers.
5. FLAG THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT against every recommendation. If a method's evidence base comes from 300+ basins, say so explicitly and assess whether it can work at n=19.
6. ACQUISITION CONSTRAINT: recommend only free/public data, or data obtainable by a reasonable request (e.g. emailing IIHR or Iowa DNR). No paid datasets, no field campaigns, no new sensor deployment.
7. Prefer peer-reviewed literature and authoritative agency sources over blog posts. Give DOIs where they exist.
8. JUDGE EVERYTHING AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. State plainly when a method only works at gauged sites.


## Your assignment: synthesize the findings for angle "Basin attributes that explain cross-site mean nitrate in tile-drained corn belt catchments"

### Research question
In peer-reviewed Midwest/Corn Belt studies, which STATIC basin attributes explain cross-site variance in mean or exceedance-frequency stream nitrate concentration, and with what partial effect sizes? For each attribute, does a downloadable, basin-aggregatable dataset covering Iowa (and neighboring states) exist?

### What a good answer contains
A table of candidate attributes - artificial/tile drainage extent, baseflow index, soil drainage class and hydrologic soil group (SSURGO), depth to water table, subsurface residence/transit time proxies, riparian buffer and wetland fraction, stream/drainage density, tile-weighted N surplus, manure vs commercial N split, soil organic N - each with reported effect size and direction, plus the specific dataset (name, resolution, years, URL, access, license). MUST resolve tile drainage concretely: check Valayamkunnath et al. 2020 (30 m CONUS tile drainage map), Nakagaki & Wieczorek USGS drainage layers, Sugg 2007 (drained agricultural land), and USDA NASS Ag Census county tile acreage. MUST also address the N-surplus 2017 cliff: is there a post-2017 continuation, an alternative N-input product (USGS county-level N fertilizer/manure estimates - Falcone, Brakebill/Gronberg), or a defensible argument for using surplus as a STATIC basin attribute (a basin's rank is stable over time) rather than as a broadcast time series - note the failed broadcast experiment does NOT rule out the static-rank use.

### TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED claims
These were extracted from real sources but were NEVER adversarially verified - verification was cut to conserve budget. The characteristic failure mode in this corpus is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE, not fabrication: a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed.

STRICT RULES for tier 3, which you MUST follow:
- USE them for COVERAGE and LEADS: naming a dataset, a URL, an access route, a candidate attribute, or an angle worth pursuing.
- DO NOT use them as the warrant for any numeric performance figure, any effect size, or the core argument of any recommendation. Those must rest on verified (tier 1) claims.
- Any finding that rests on tier 3 MUST set confidence to "unverified" and say so in the claim text itself.
- If a tier 3 claim contradicts a verified claim, the verified claim wins; note the conflict.

Produce the structured finding set for this angle as JSON.

Merge semantic duplicates. Apply every correction supplied by the verifiers. Rank findings by relevance to the BETWEEN-SITE gap specifically. For each finding give feasibilityAtN19 and worksAtUngaugedPin honestly. Populate "datasets" for every concrete data source, with howToIncorporate written concretely enough to act on - name the feature that would be created and how it would be aggregated to a basin. Populate "uncovered" for any part of the question that produced nothing verifiable - absence of evidence must be reported as absence, never silently dropped. Your "verdict" must state plainly whether this angle is worth pursuing and why.

Output JSON with keys: angle, verdict, findings[] (each: claim, confidence, effectSize, splitProtocol, nBasins, sources[], feasibilityAtN19, worksAtUngaugedPin), datasets[] (each: name, url, resolution, years, access, license, coversMultiState, whyUseful, howToIncorporate, limitations), refuted[], uncovered[].

tier1_survived.claim: AgTile-US is a 30-m resolution binary raster (0 = undrained cropland, 1 = tile-drained cropland) covering the entire contiguous United States (65°20'W–127°53'W, 22°51'N–51°36'N), reference year 2017. It is a SINGLE STATIC SNAPSHOT — the authors explicitly state it 'does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation.' Falsifiable operational consequence: it can supply a per-basin tile-drainage-fraction as a STATIC basin attribute (one number per basin, exactly the between-site static information the LOFO gap needs), but it cannot supply any time-varying tile signal. Because it is CONUS-wide, it also covers the multi-state portions of Iowa basins, unlike the Iowa-only CDL/N-surplus joins that currently under-count area for the largest basins.
tier1_survived.effectSize: 30 m resolution; 22,340,442 ha tile-drained CONUS; Iowa 5,706,831 ha (largest of any state); reference year 2017; binary 0/1
corrections:
The claim is substantively correct and operationally usable; three corrections and one caution.

(1) MISQUOTE. The sentence attributed verbatim to the authors ("does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation") is not in the paper. Replace with the actual text: "The data deliver a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017." The claim's conclusion - static snapshot, cannot supply any time-varying tile signal - is nonetheless correct.

(2) IT IS A MODELED PRODUCT, NOT AN OBSERVATION, AND THIS IS THE MAIN THREAT TO THE CLAIM'S CENTRAL ARGUMENT. AgTile-US is a deterministic decision tree over SSURGO soil drainage category and SRTM slope, thresholded until accumulated area matches USDA COUNTY-level census tile acreage. The per-basin tile fraction is therefore a smooth function of soil drainage class and slope, constrained only at county granularity. The claim asserts this is "exactly the between-site static information the LOFO gap needs." At n=19 independent basin families in Iowa, that new attribute may be substantially collinear with lat/lon - already the #2 and #3 features by permutation importance - and with the CDL crop fractions. It is not guaranteed to be independent information. Before assuming lift, compute the correlation of basin tile-fraction against lat, lon, log_basin_area and the CDL bucket features; if R^2 against existing statics is high, expected gain is small.

(3) DENOMINATOR AMBIGUITY - the claim says "one number per basin" but there are two distinct features. Non-agricultural land is MASKED OUT, not coded 0, so (a) tile cells / total basin cells and (b) tile cells / agricultural cells are different quantities. (b) is drainage intensity, the physically meaningful control; (a) conflates drainage with crop cover already captured by the 8 CDL classes x 3 buckets. Build both; they are not interchangeable. Also note the mask is NLCD-2016 cropland, a different land-cover product from the CDL currently used, so cell-level agreement with existing crop features is imperfect.

(4) CAUTION, NOT A BLOCKER, ON THE 2017 DATE. This is superficially the same 2017 endpoint as the N-surplus product whose forward-broadcast failed badly (-0.166). The failure modes differ: that was a TIME-VARYING feature held constant, whereas this is used as a static basin attribute where no temporal claim is made. Tile installation is also far more inertial than annual nitrogen application, so a 2017 snapshot is a defensible constant across 2008-2026. Do not treat the prior negative result as predicting failure here, but do enter it as a static attribute only - never as a per-day feature.

FIT TO THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: clean. It is a raster, so it is computable for an arbitrary map pin's NLDI-delineated basin with no local nitrate history, no discharge gauge, and no monitored upstream neighbor. It requires nothing from the target site's own observations. FIT TO n=19: unusually good - one additional static scalar is affordable at 19 effective units in a way a large catchment-attribute set is not. Iowa mapping accuracy (91.1%) is above the CONUS average.

The claim is substantively correct and every quantitative figure is exact. Three corrections. (1) The sentence "does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation" is presented as a verbatim authors' quote but could not be located in the paper; the paper's actual wording is "The data deliver a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017." The meaning is right, the quotation is not. (2) The 0/1 classes are defined over an NLCD-2016 agricultural mask, not CDL cropland, and the paper flags 18.15% under-representation of CONUS croplands in NLCD-2016 - so basin tile fraction must be computed against basin area or AgTile-US's own domain, never as a ratio to our CDL crop-cell counts. (3) Omitted and important: AgTile-US is a downscaling of county-level USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture drained-acreage totals, allocated within county by SSURGO drainage class and SRTM slope via a decision tree. Its 30 m grid is a rendering resolution, not an information resolution; its true independent unit is the county, and within a county it is a deterministic function of soils and slope. It therefore adds little beyond SSURGO drainage class + basin slope, and carries roughly +/-19.8% inherited census error. Recommended use stands - one static per-basin attribute, obtainable at an arbitrary ungauged pin, CC-BY, DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742 - but the decisive test is whether it improves LOFO CONDITIONAL on lat/lon, which may already proxy the Des Moines Lobe tile gradient.

Claim is accurate and should be accepted, with four precisions. (1) QUOTE INEXACT: the phrase "does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation" is presented as an author quote but conflates two distinct caveats. The paper's temporal caveat reads "a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017"; the spatial caveat is separate and different - "each 30-m grid identified as tile drained is entirely tile drained", i.e. presence/absence only, no sub-pixel drainage density. The operational conclusion (static basin attribute only, no time-varying tile signal) is nonetheless correct. (2) MODELED, NOT OBSERVED: AgTile-US is derived from SSURGO soil drainage class + SRTM slope threshold + CDL cropland mask, calibrated to county-level USDA Census tile acreage. The near-match of the 22,340,442 ha total to the 22,418,966 ha Census figure is therefore close to tautological at national scale and is NOT independent validation; the independent evidence is the 16,000-point photo-interpretation (86.03% pixel accuracy). Basin-aggregated fractions should be more accurate than 86% since independent pixel errors partly cancel - this favors the intended use. (3) COLLINEARITY RISK, the main reason to temper expectations: because the product is a deterministic function of soil drainage class, slope and cropland, and because Iowa tile drainage is spatially concentrated in the Des Moines Lobe, a per-basin tile fraction will partly duplicate information that lat/lon (already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features) encode. The feature should be benchmarked explicitly against a lat/lon-only baseline, not just against the current model. (4) n=19 FLAG: this adds a single static column evaluated against ~19 effective independent basin families. That is the mildest form of the sample-size constraint - one degree of freedom, not a 300-basin architecture - but a single spurious alignment across 19 units can still masquerade as a win, so any LOFO gain should be checked for stability under leave-one-family-out perturbation. Also note AgTile-US fixes the multi-state under-count for the tile variable only; the CDL and N-surplus joins remain Iowa-truncated.

tier1_survived.claim: AgTile-US is not an independent observation of tile drainage: it is a geospatial decision-tree DOWNSCALING of USDA Census of Agriculture 2017 county-level tile acreage, allocated to pixels by SSURGO v2.0 soil drainage class (7 categories, iterated D=7 down to D=1) within an NLCD 2016 cropland mask, subject to a topographic slope threshold (0% to 20% max) from SRTM. Falsifiable consequence for this project: a basin-aggregated AgTile fraction will be strongly collinear with basin-aggregated SSURGO drainage class, mean slope, and county cropland fraction — so adding AgTile fraction AND SSURGO hydrologic-soil-group/drainage-class as separate features is largely redundant, and any measured gain should be attributed to the composite, not to three independent attributes. Aggregate CONUS area matched the census to −0.35% (22.34 vs 22.42 Mha) by construction.
tier1_survived.effectSize: Inputs: USDA Ag Census 2017 county tile acreage; SSURGO v2.0 drainage class (7 classes); NLCD 2016 cropland; SRTM slope (0–20% threshold). Aggregate deviation from census: −0.35%
corrections:
The claim is factually exact on inputs, algorithm, and the -0.35% / 22.34 vs 22.42 Mha figures, and its collinearity warning is operationally sound. Two corrections:

(1) "Not an independent observation of tile drainage" is too strong on both ends. The county input IS an observation — USDA Census of Agriculture farmer-reported tile acreage — and the paper reports genuine INDEPENDENT validation the claim omits entirely: 16,000 tile-drainage ground-truth points manually identified from ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery (15 m / 1 m / 0.6 m / 0.3 m) across ten states, giving 86.03% overall accuracy for CONUS (13.97% omission), 82.7-93.6% across the tile-drained Midwest, and 91.1% for IOWA specifically on 5,253 ground-truth points, with >98% accuracy in poorly drained soils and errors concentrated in marginal drainage categories 3-5. For this project's Iowa-basin use case that is the number that matters, and it is good. AgTile-US should be described as a census-constrained downscaling that has been independently validated at 91.1% in Iowa, not as an unvalidated composite.

(2) The redundancy is exact WITHIN a county but not ACROSS counties. Because the county census acreage enters as a per-county calibration constant, two counties with identical SSURGO drainage-class and slope distributions and identical cropland fraction receive DIFFERENT tile fractions whenever their census acreages differ. So basin-aggregated AgTile fraction carries county-scale information that is not recoverable from SSURGO + slope + NLCD alone; it is not a pure function of them. Practical consequence, which strengthens rather than weakens the claim's advice: add AgTile fraction as a single static per-bucket feature and do NOT also add the SSURGO drainage-class histogram or mean slope as separate features — they are the ingredients, not independent evidence. Also note the product is BINARY extent (drained yes/no, "does not distinguish drainage intensity/spacing"), so it proxies drained AREA, not the drainage DENSITY the project brief names as the dominant Iowa hydrologic control.

Two corrections, both to interpretation rather than to the quoted facts.

(1) THE CENTRAL MECHANISTIC ERROR. AgTile-US is NOT a deterministic function of SSURGO drainage class + slope + cropland alone, so the strong-collinearity prediction is overstated. The paper states: "thresholds of slope and soil drainage properties were estimated separately for each county." The county-specific (D*, S*) thresholds are set by that county's Ag Census tile acreage. Two counties with identical soil-drainage histograms, identical slope distributions and identical cropland fraction but different reported census tile acreage receive DIFFERENT thresholds and different tiled fractions. Basin-aggregated AgTile fraction is therefore f(soils, slope, cropland, COUNTY CENSUS TILE ACREAGE) — and that last term is genuine, independent, survey-derived information about human drainage investment that is not recoverable from any raster in the current feature set. The claim's "any measured gain should be attributed to the composite, not to three independent attributes" should be corrected to: the gain should be attributed to the composite, and the composite's non-redundant content is the county census acreage signal, which is exactly the between-site static information this project is missing.

(2) "Not an independent observation" is right about provenance but should be stated alongside the independent accuracy validation (16,000 photo-interpreted points, 86.03% CONUS overall accuracy, 13.97% omission, 82.7–93.6% in Midwest states). The construction is a downscaling; the product is nonetheless independently validated as skillful at the pixel level.

PRACTICAL GUIDANCE THAT SURVIVES: the operational advice is still sound — prefer basin-mean AgTile fraction as a SINGLE feature over adding AgTile + SSURGO drainage class + mean slope as three, because at ~19 independent basin families the correlated-static budget is tiny. But add one caveat the claim does not raise: because thresholds are solved per county, AgTile-US has DISCONTINUITIES AT COUNTY LINES. Basin-aggregated values inherit a county-mosaic step artifact, worst for basins spanning many counties and for the multi-state basins. Sanity-check basin AgTile fraction against county boundaries before trusting between-site rank ordering derived from it.

The claim is directionally correct and its quoted numbers are exact, but it overstates redundancy in two specific ways that change what you should do with it.

(1) "NOT AN INDEPENDENT OBSERVATION" IS TOO ABSOLUTE. The pixel ALLOCATION is pure downscaling, as claimed. But one genuinely exogenous observation does enter: the USDA county-level tile acreage itself is farmer-reported survey data, not derived from soil or terrain. AgTile encodes, per county, WHERE ON THE (drainage-class, slope) ORDERING THE CUTOFF FALLS — and that cutoff is set by real reported acreage that cannot be recovered from gSSURGO + NLCD + SRTM alone. So AgTile fraction is not a deterministic function of the other three candidate features; it is those three features PLUS a county-resolution intensity signal. Practical consequence for this project: WITHIN a county, AgTile variation is pure soil+slope and is fully redundant. BETWEEN counties, AgTile carries real information. Since Iowa basins typically span many counties, the between-county component is where any genuine gain would come from — and that is exactly the between-site term where the project's headroom lies. Do not dismiss the feature; dismiss the triple-counting.

(2) The paper DID conduct an accuracy assessment against non-census data — 16,000 manually interpreted aerial-imagery points, 86.03% overall CONUS accuracy, 13.97% omission error — which the claim omits entirely. However, this assessment is compromised rather than absent: the same points calibrated the 20% slope threshold, and no held-out split is described, so treat 86.03% as an optimistic in-sample figure. State-level breakdowns (an Iowa-specific figure near 91% on roughly 5,000 points) came back inconsistent across two extraction passes and should be read directly from the paper's tables before being cited.

(3) Minor precision fixes: the soil input is GRIDDED SSURGO (gSSURGO) v2.0, native 10-m resampled to 30-m, not vector SSURGO; and the D-loop terminates when the county census target is exceeded, so D=1 is the floor of the search rather than a step every county reaches.

RECOMMENDED ACTION: add AgTile-US basin fraction as a single static feature; do NOT simultaneously add SSURGO drainage-class and mean-slope basin summaries as if they were independent attributes. If you want to test whether AgTile adds anything beyond terrain and soil, the clean ablation is AgTile-fraction versus (drainage-class + slope + cropland-fraction) as competing feature sets under the same LOFO protocol, not both together — and expect the discriminating signal to be between-county, so check whether it survives at n=19 families before believing it.

License is Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0) with metadata under CC0 — free for commercial use with attribution, so it is shippable in a deployed product. The GEE asset means a per-basin tile fraction can be computed on the fly for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated map-pin basin via a reduceRegion call, with no local raster storage — directly compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target.
tier1_survived.effectSize: DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742; GEE asset projects/sat-io/open-datasets/agtile/AgTile-US; formats GeoTIFF + NetCDF-4; CC-BY 4.0; no auth required
corrections:
The claim is accurate on every identifier and should be acted on, but four corrections matter, one of them material.

1. MATERIAL — the "no authentication / free for commercial use / shippable" chain is valid for Figshare and INVALID for the GEE path. The claim correctly establishes CC-BY 4.0 on the data, then attaches that to the Earth Engine delivery mechanism. Earth Engine is a separate licensing regime from the dataset: it requires a Google account and a registered Google Cloud project (authentication, contradicting "NO authentication" for that path), and Google's Earth Engine FAQ states it "is free for noncommercial use" while directing "commercial or operational applications" to paid Cloud pricing. A deployed public-facing product is an operational application. So AgTile-US-via-GEE is NOT free-and-unauthenticated for the shipped product; AgTile-US-via-Figshare is.

2. The GEE asset is an ee.Image (the catalog loads it as a single Image), not an ImageCollection — the claim's hedge resolves to Image. It is also a community mirror maintained under samapriya's sat-io project, not an official NCAR or Google-curated asset, so its persistence is not guaranteed by the data producer.

3. The "no local raster storage" framing is backwards for this deployment target. The CONUS GeoTIFF is 126 MB zipped — trivial to vendor. Local storage is strictly superior here: no auth, no EE quota, no per-request latency, no third-party runtime dependency, and it dodges correction (1) entirely. A 30 m reduceRegion over a large multi-state NLDI basin is a seconds-to-minutes call subject to EE timeouts, on the critical path of every map-pin request. RECOMMENDATION: bulk-download the GeoTIFF from Figshare and compute basin tile fraction locally with the existing basin-cell machinery. Reserve GEE for prototyping only.

4. Fitness for this project (the claim does not overstate, but the ceiling should be stated). Genuine strengths: it is CONUS-wide, so unlike the Iowa-truncated CDL/N-surplus inner join it correctly covers the multi-state portions of the largest basins — it fixes that known under-counting bug for this one variable. It is binary at 30 m, so "mean over basin cells" is a clean, well-defined tile fraction. And it is a purely STATIC between-site covariate, which is precisely the class that has worked on this project (geometry + static geography) rather than the temporal class that has failed seven times. Iowa validation accuracy is 91.1%.

Caveats to carry: (a) n=19 FAMILIES — this variable moves only between sites, so it is evaluated against ~19 effective independent units. Add ONE basin-wide tile fraction first, not three distance-bucketed copies; the bucketed version spends three degrees of freedom on a between-site term that has ~19 points, and the riparian-bucket result (CLF +0.039 PR-AUC, REG worse) shows bucketing static geography is not reliably free. (b) It is a MODELED product that downscales county-level Ag Census totals using NLCD cropland + slope + SSURGO drainage class, not observed tile locations. It is therefore a soils-plus-cropland-plus-census composite and may be partly collinear with existing CDL crop-fraction features — expect a smaller incremental gain than "the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa" suggests. (c) It is single-year 2017 held constant across 2008-2026. This superficially resembles the known failure "broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward (-0.166)", but differs in kind: N surplus is a genuinely time-varying flux, whereas tile infrastructure is near-static on decadal timescales, so a constant value is defensible. That prior failure is still a reason to test rather than assume.

Directionally correct; three corrections, one of which invalidates the recommended deployment path.

(A) THE GEE PATH IS NOT AUTH-FREE AND IS NOT FREE FOR A COMMERCIAL PRODUCT. This is the claim's one real error. "No authentication required" and "free for commercial use, so shippable in a deployed product" are true of the Figshare download, but the claim chains them onto the GEE reduceRegion deployment story. Google's own docs: "To use Earth Engine you'll need access to a Cloud project that: has the Earth Engine API enabled, is registered for commercial or noncommercial use" (developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/access), and the FAQ states "Earth Engine is free for noncommercial use" with commercial/operational applications directed to paid Google Cloud pricing. Projects registered before 2025-04-15 must verify noncommercial eligibility. 3. FILE SIZES AND FORMAT. Zip is 12,107,588 bytes (11.5 MiB), not "13 MB". Uncompressed is 139,700,008 bytes (133 MiB), not "154 MB". The member file is TILES92_CONUS.txt (comma-delimited, .txt extension), not a .csv.

4. "EVERY TABLE SUPPLIES THREE SPATIAL AGGREGATIONS" IS FALSE AS A UNIVERSAL. The parent summary states FOUR spatial components, not three: reach catchments, riparian buffer zones, network-accumulated catchments, network-accumulated riparian buffers. Several child items ship only one aggregation: the ClimGRID water-balance items are split into separate items per routing type ("per Flowline Catchment" / "Using Divergence Routing" / "Using Total Upstream Routing"), and riparian items (e.g. "NLCD 2001 Percent Imperviousness in 100 Meter Riparian Buffer") are buffer-only. Others split CAT/ACC/TOT into separate zips within one item — e.g. "Select Topographic Attributes: Select Basin Attributes" ships BASIN_CHAR_CAT_CONUS.zip (50.4 MB), BASIN_CHAR_ACC_CONUS.zip (55.0 MB), BASIN_CHAR_TOT_CONUS.zip (57.2 MB) as three separate downloads. Budget for per-item schema discovery; do not assume one zip = one 7-column table.

5. CC0 IS NOT STATED ON THE RECORD. The ScienceBase JSON `rights` field is null for both the parent and the tile item; no occurrence of "CC0", "Creative Commons", "public domain", or "license" anywhere in either JSON or in the FGDC XML. The XML carries only a liability disclaimer and "Use of this data is considered acceptance of the limitations of this data." The data are almost certainly free to use (USGS-authored, 17 U.S.C. 105), but "License: CC0 1.0 Universal" is an inference the cited source does not support. Cite it as a USGS public-domain data release, not CC0.

6. "ALL ATTRIBUTES ARE STATIC SINGLE-EPOCH SNAPSHOTS" IS FALSE — and the truth is better for this project. Many child items are multi-epoch: NLCD 2019 version supplies 2001/2004/2006/2008/2011/2013/2016/2019; housing density 1940-2010; block-level population density 1990/2000/2010; CDL as separate 2012/2013/2014 items; monthly PRISM and ClimGRID series. That means some of these can be used as slowly-varying covariates, not only as static ones.

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS THE CLAIM OMITS, ALL MATERIAL TO THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET:

A. THE PIN LOOKUP IS SIMPLER THAN THE CLAIM SAYS. The claim hedges "provided the pin's basin can be decomposed into NHDPlusV2 COMIDs." Not needed. TOT_ and ACC_ are already the accumulated upstream value at that reach, so the deployment path is: NLDI resolves the pin to one outlet COMID (this repo already does exactly that — /Users/isaac/dev/sustag/deploy/build_virtual_basin.py and /Users/isaac/dev/sustag/src/build/_make_basins.py both already call NLDI for the enclosing COMID), then one hash lookup into the table. No basin decomposition, no zonal statistics, no local history. This is a genuinely deployment-compatible static feature source — the strongest part of the claim.

B. THE TILE LAYER IS 1992 AND COARSE — a serious caveat the claim does not mention. FGDC process step: source is "Downloaded the source data from http://water.usgs.gov/GIS/metadata/usgswrd/XML/nri92_cp606.xml", i.e. Wieczorek (2004) "Estimated area of artificial drainage for the year 1992", derived from the 1992 National Resources Inventory Conservation Practice 606 — an expanded statistical sample, not a mapped drainage network. The metadata's own use constraint, verbatim: "One should use caution and read this document before using these data to estimate smaller areas. These data should not be used for site-specific evaluation, surveying, or engineering purposes. They should also not be used beyond the limits of the source data's scale." Iowa tile drainage has expanded materially since 1992. Validation was only a spot check: "Basin metrics were spot checked by randomly creating a set of basins across the country... Results demonstrated the process performed correctly" — no quantitative accuracy statistic, and "No formal positional accuracy tests were conducted." So this resolves the project's "no tile drainage data source identified" gap only partially: it gives a plausible relative ranking of basins by drainage intensity, not a defensible absolute percentage.

C. n=19 CONSTRAINT. This release has no effect size and no split protocol — it is a data source, not a study, so rules 1/2/5 apply to how it is used, not to the claim. Judged against n=19 independent basin families: adding one TOT_TILES92 scalar is a single between-site covariate against ~19 effective units. That is the right shape for the diagnosed between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21) and is affordable. The danger is the obvious next move — this release offers 158 tables and easily thousands of TOT_ columns. Bulk-joining them and letting XGBoost pick creates a p >> 19 selection problem where LOFO will select on noise across folds. Recommend a pre-registered handful (tile drainage, STATSGO hydrologic group / soil restrictive layer, base flow index, topographic wetness index, basin slope, N from fertilizer+manure) chosen on hydrologic reasoning before seeing LOFO scores, not a wide sweep.

D. STRUCTURAL CHURN RISK. Parent provenance, verbatim: "2026-03-26: The structure of this data release has been updated to support migration to a new USGS data system." The broken parquet URLs are almost certainly collateral from that migration. Pin the downloaded files locally; do not build a live-fetch dependency on the ?f=__disk__<sha> URLs, which are content-addressed and can change.

E. FGDC METADATA BUG. In the tile table's entity-attribute list, the third variable is labeled "ACC_TILES92" a second time where the actual header says TOT_TILES92. Anyone auto-generating a schema from the XML will produce a duplicate key. Parse the CSV header, not the XML.

tier1_refuted.claim: AgTile-US validation against 16,000 manually-identified ground-truth points from ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery (0.3–15 m) gave 86.03% overall CONUS accuracy with 13.97% omission error; over the heavily tile-drained Midwest accuracy ranged 82.7%–93.6%, and IOWA SPECIFICALLY scored 91.1% on 5,253 ground-truth points. This is the highest per-state validation density in the paper, so an Iowa-basin tile fraction derived from this raster carries roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification — a per-basin aggregate would average much of that out, making basin-level tile fraction a low-noise attribute.
why:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED, EXACT. Source is Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7, at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406500/. All quoted figures match verbatim: "Validation of AgTile-US with 16000 ground truth points indicated 86.03% accuracy at the CONUS-scale"; "The AgTile-US failed to identify tile drainage at about 13.97% of ground-truth locations"; "Over the heavily tile-drained midwestern regions of the U.S., the accuracy ranges from 82.7% to 93.6%"; "Iowa (5.7 Mha), where we have identified 5253 ground truth points, and the AgTile-US showed 91.1% accuracy." ESRI multi-resolution basemap (15 m, 1 m, 0.6 m, 0.3 m) confirmed; imagery dates 10/2/2012-4/23/2017. No misattribution or exaggeration in the numbers themselves.

THE INFERENCE IS REFUTED ON THREE GROUNDS, ALL FROM THE PAPER'S OWN TEXT.

(1) POSITIVE-ONLY VALIDATION; COMMISSION ERROR NEVER MEASURED. Authors: "We limited the tile drainage ground-truth identification mostly to fallow croplands where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable," and list "uncertainty in croplands without tile drainage" as a primary limitation of the validation approach. The 16,000 points are tile-drained locations only. Hence 86.03%/91.1% are producer's accuracy (recall) for the tile class, NOT balanced overall accuracy. False-positive rate is unreported and unmeasurable from this design. The claim's "roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification" is therefore incorrect: it is ~8.9% OMISSION among visually-confirmed tiled parcels, plus an unknown commission rate. A map over-painting tile drainage across untiled cropland would score identically.

(2) NON-RANDOM SAMPLE. Points restricted to fallow fields where tile signatures are visible in imagery, so even the omission rate does not generalize to the pixel population.

(3) DECISIVE: ERROR STRUCTURE IS COUNTY-BLOCKED, SO AGGREGATION DOES NOT AVERAGE IT OUT. AgTile-US is not an independent per-pixel classifier. It is a deterministic downscaling that allocates USDA Census of Agriculture 2017 COUNTY-LEVEL tile area totals onto NLCD-2016 cropland pixels via SSURGO v2.0 drainage class (7 categories) and SRTM 30 m slope, iterating the slope threshold (1% steps, then 0.1% refinement) until the county total is matched. Errors are spatially correlated at county scale by construction. Authors quantify the binding constraint: "The average error in tile drainage estimates based on the Census of Agriculture 2017 is 19.8%," and state "Any uncertainty in these datasets will lead to inaccuracies in the model estimated tile drainage map." Basin-level aggregation averages WITHIN-county placement error but inherits the ~19.8% county census error essentially undiluted, since an Iowa basin spans few counties. Aggregation averages independent noise; it cannot average out systematic bias. The claim's central assertion — "a per-basin aggregate would average much of that out, making basin-level tile fraction a low-noise attribute" — is thus unsupported and directionally wrong.

ADDITIONAL: NLCD-2016 underrepresents census cropland by -18.15% CONUS, compounding the project's known inner-join undercount for multi-state basins. Map is a static 2017 snapshot (not time-varying). Sub-claim "highest per-state validation density in the paper" is UNVERIFIED: Iowa has the highest point COUNT (5,253/16,000 = 33%), but per-state results appear only in Fig. 5f without a full tabular breakdown, and points-per-cropland-area density is not established; other states span 72.8%-100%.

TRANSFERABILITY (dataset survives, claim does not): AgTile-US is free, public, 30 m, CONUS-wide, and is a STATIC BETWEEN-SITE basin attribute — precisely the deficit class where this project's remaining headroom lies (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21), and it is computable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history, satisfying the deployment target. Static-2017 is acceptable here because the intended use is a static site attribute, not a temporal driver. CONUS coverage handles multi-state basin portions. n=19 CAVEAT: with only 19 independent basin families, adding one static predictor carrying ~20% county-correlated error risks fitting census artifact rather than tile signal; gains must be demonstrated under LOFO, not in-sample.

PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED. Cited URL resolves to Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data. All four headline numbers are quoted verbatim and exactly: "an overall accuracy of 86.03% for the CONUS" "with an omission error of 13.97%"; "manually identified 16000 tile drainage ground-truth points across ten states...from the ESRI multi-resolution (15 m, 1 m, 0.6 m, and 0.3 m) aerial imagery basemap"; "Over the heavily tile-drained midwestern regions of the U.S., the accuracy ranges from 82.7% to 93.6%"; "The state with the most tile drained croplands is Iowa (5.7 Mha), where we have identified 5253 ground truth points, and the AgTile-US showed 91.1% accuracy." No misattribution or garbling of the numbers.

REFUTATION RESTS ON THREE METHODOLOGICAL DEFECTS, NOT ON THE NUMBERS.

(1) METRIC MISREAD - the load-bearing error. The 16,000 ground-truth points are POSITIVES ONLY (tile-drained locations). The paper reports no confirmed non-drained control points, no confusion matrix, no kappa, no user's accuracy, and NO COMMISSION ERROR anywhere. Sampling was additionally non-random and best-case by design: the authors "limited the tile drainage ground-truth identification mostly to fallow croplands where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable." The arithmetic confirms single-class recall: 86.03 + 13.97 = 100.00 exactly. Therefore 86.03%/91.1% are producer's accuracy (recall) on a detectability-biased positive subsample, NOT overall pixel classification accuracy. The claim's inference that the Iowa raster "carries roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification" is unsupported: the false-positive rate is unmeasured in the source, so total pixel misclassification is unbounded from above by anything the paper reports.

(2) VALIDATION IS IN-SAMPLE; the claim's "split protocol: not-applicable" is affirmatively false. Verbatim: "To validate the AgTile-US and to set the upper limit of slope in the geospatial model, we have manually identified 16000 ground-truth points," and "Using the extracted slope values, we have identified the upper limit of slope (=20%) in the geospatial model." The same points that set a model threshold were used to report accuracy. Separately, the map is iteratively CONSTRAINED to county-level USDA census tile acreage, so the Table 1 county-level agreement (-0.35% CONUS) is circular by construction and is not independent corroboration.

(3) AGGREGATION ARGUMENT ASSUMES THE WRONG ERROR STRUCTURE. "A per-basin aggregate would average much of that out" is valid only for independent random pixel error. AgTile-US is a GIS decision tree over SSURGO v2.0 soil drainage class and SRTM-derived slope, with NLCD-2016 cropland; its errors are inherited from soil map-unit polygons and terrain and are therefore spatially structured at scales comparable to a basin. Systematic/correlated error does not average out with area - it becomes a persistent PER-BASIN BIAS, which is exactly the between-site term (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24) the project is trying to improve. The claim's conclusion ("low-noise attribute") thus does not follow even from its own premise.

(4) UNVERIFIABLE SUB-CLAIM. "Highest per-state validation density in the paper" cannot be checked: the paper publishes no per-state point breakdown beyond Iowa (Figure 5f references nine other states without counts). Iowa plausibly has the highest COUNT (5253/16000 = 32.8%), but density per unit area is not computable. Also note 91.1% is not the Midwest maximum; 93.6% belongs to an unnamed state.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT (independent of the refutation). The underlying recommendation to use AgTile-US survives on other grounds. Operational and compliant with the acquisition constraint: Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, GeoTIFF and NetCDF-4, 30 m resolution, static single epoch representing 2017, full CONUS extent, CC BY 4.0 (metadata CC0), no authentication, code at https://github.com/NCAR/AgTile-US. CONUS coverage directly addresses the known inner-join defect for multi-state basins. It is also the correct CLASS of feature for this project: a static between-site attribute, matching the only pattern that has produced wins (geometry and static geography) rather than the temporal class that has failed seven times. The county-census constraint is in fact a stronger argument for basin-AGGREGATE reliability than the point validation the claim invokes, though it does not license a pixel-level noise figure. BINDING RISK is n=19 independent basin families, not pixel noise: a per-basin tile fraction is an additional static covariate likely collinear with lat/lon (already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features), and at 19 effective units it can appear informative in-fold while contributing nothing in transfer. It should be tested as a replacement for, not an addition to, existing static geography, and any LOFO gain treated as provisional. Note also the 2017 static epoch is the same vintage as the N-surplus product whose forward-broadcast already failed (-0.166); as a time-invariant basin attribute this is not the same failure mode, but the 2017 snapshot cannot represent drainage expansion across the 2008-2026 record.

This is a near-exact scale match to the Iowa virtual-sensor project (~85 sites, 160,074 site-days), so its results are the closest published analogue available and its failure modes should be treated as directly transferable rather than as evidence from a large-sample regime.

tier3_unverified.claim: In the same study, an LSTM predicting daily nitrate CONCENTRATION scored median KGE = 0.60 under TEMPORAL validation (held-out time period at sites the model had seen) but only median KGE = 0.18 under SPATIAL validation (prediction in unmonitored basins, i.e. the true PUB / ungauged setting), rising to median KGE = 0.34 when the spatial-validation evaluation was restricted to Mississippi River Basin sites. (2020, Scientific Data 7:257, doi:10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x). (2025) used Shapley dependence to identify quantitative NON-LINEAR THRESHOLDS in watershed attributes beyond which they begin to exert considerable influence on river nitrate, and framed the intervention question explicitly as 'given a watershed in Iowa with 60% tile drainage and 5% wetland cover, what would predicted nitrate be if tile drain density were reduced from 60% to 0% or wetland cover doubled from 5% to 10%'. tier3_unverified.claim: Applying spatially-validated flow and nitrate LSTMs across the Mississippi River Basin for 1980-2022, Pandit et al. (2025) found riverine nitrate export equal to only 19 +/- 4% of N SURPLUS on average, but that this export fraction is strongly wetness-dependent: 42 +/- 24% of surplus in WET years versus 6 +/- 6% in DRY years for Midwestern states - a roughly 7x swing. It simultaneously supports the alternative use the project has not yet tested - N surplus as a STATIC basin attribute (a basin's surplus RANK, entered once) interacted with a wetness term - since surplus clearly does control export magnitude once hydrologic conditions are conditioned on.

tier3_unverified.claim: This paper regressed 2017 stream nitrate against 2012 agricultural-census-derived N inputs (commercial fertilizer from USGS NAWQA 2012; county manure N from Gronberg & Arnold 2017 for 2012) and obtained its significant relationships anyway - a direct precedent for using N inputs as a STATIC basin-rank attribute across a 5-year offset rather than as a time-matched series. The report's own stated use constraint is temporal and scale-based, not rank-based: 'For use as a time series, these data are best suited for use in multicounty or regional analysis', and the FGDC metadata useconst reads verbatim 'Data are best suited for use at multi-county or regional scales'. This is an explicit agency warning that single-county, single-year values are the weakest use — the source discourages fine temporal reading while endorsing aggregation, the opposite polarity from a broadcast time series.

tier3_unverified.claim: Gorski et al. (2024) predicted the backward-looking 7-day-average stream nitrate concentration at 46 predominantly agricultural sites in the midwestern/eastern US with LSTM models, and the headline skill number — 'median Kling-Gupta Efficiency = 0.66' — comes from SINGLE-SITE models 'in which models are trained and tested at a single location' (verbatim abstract). No site was spatially held out, so this paper provides NO evidence of transfer to an unmonitored basin and its 0.66 KGE is NOT comparable to our LOFO numbers. Every one of the 46 sites is a USGS gauge and daily discharge (NWIS code 00060) is a required model input, so the entire modeling design is inapplicable to an arbitrary ungauged map pin (we have discharge at only 22 of 85 sites, zero of 61 IWQIS sites).

tier3_unverified.claim: Gorski et al. (2024) report a direct NEGATIVE result on pooling sites: 'Developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model,' and they add 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' Accuracy at poorly performing sites was instead improved by GROUPING sites with similar characteristics (the data release carries a 'cluster' and a 'hydro_terrane' label per site). This is peer-reviewed evidence that for nitrate specifically, the CAMELS-style 'one big multi-basin model wins' result does not automatically hold — and it argues for similarity-grouped models rather than one global model. Caveat for us: with 19 independent basin families, splitting into similarity clusters leaves ~4-6 families per cluster, which is likely too few to fit separate models; the actionable version is cluster/terrane membership as a FEATURE, not as a model partition.

tier3_unverified.claim: Gorski et al. (2024) represented nitrogen inputs to their 46 basins as STATIC, SINGLE-VINTAGE attributes rather than as a time series: TOT_N97 is defined verbatim as 'estimate of nitrogen from fertilizer and manure in 1997' and fert_uN_mt_sqkm as 'nitrogen fertilizer use'. This is direct precedent for the defensible use our project needs: treating N surplus as a STATIC basin-rank attribute (one value per basin, no time axis) rather than broadcasting a 2017 value forward as a per-day feature. Our failed broadcast experiment (-0.166) tested the latter and does not falsify the former; the two are different features with different failure modes, and this study is evidence the static form is standard practice. It does NOT, however, provide an effect size for the N-input attributes specifically, so the value of the static form remains untested here and must be validated on our own LOFO folds.

tier3_unverified.claim: MEASURED ON THIS PROJECT'S OWN DATA (not a literature claim): the percent-subsurface-drainage attribute CAT_TILES92 (source: Wieczorek 2004, 'Subsurface Drains on Agricultural Land in the Conterminous United States, 1992: National Resource Inventory Conservation Practice 606'; ScienceBase item 57067469e4b03f95a075ad3e) was area-weighted-aggregated over each sensor basin's COMIDs and correlated against site-level nitrate computed from src/data/processed/water/data/*_water.parquet. Across n=46 sites: versus site violation rate (fraction of days with daily-max nitrate >= 10 mg/L) Pearson r=0.516 (p=0.00024, r^2=0.266), Spearman rho=0.605 (p=8.3e-06); versus site mean daily-max nitrate Pearson r=0.466 (p=0.0011, r^2=0.217), Spearman rho=0.485 (p=0.00063). In an OLS with log(basin area) as a covariate, tile percent remains significant: violation-rate model R^2=0.317 with tile coefficient 0.0055 (p=0.00138); mean-nitrate model R^2=0.296 with tile coefficient 0.0672 (p=0.00643). Direction is positive as hydrologically expected. CRITICAL CAVEAT ON PROTOCOL: this is an IN-SAMPLE cross-site correlation over all 46 sites, NOT a spatially held-out prediction, so r^2=0.266 is NOT comparable to the project's LOFO between_rate_r2 of 0.24 and will shrink under leave-one-family-out evaluation. CRITICAL CAVEAT ON SAMPLE SIZE: the 46 sites collapse to substantially fewer than the project's 19 independent basin families, so the effective independent n for this regression is well under 19 and the confidence interval on r is wide despite the small p-value. The claim to test is narrower and falsifiable: adding a single scalar tile-drainage percent as a static feature should raise LOFO between_rate_r2 above 0.24; if it does not, this correlation was driven by shared spatial autocorrelation with lat/lon, which the model already has as its 2nd and 3rd most important features.

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT — DO NOT USE THE HEADLINE 30 m TILE DRAINAGE LAYER: the Nakagaki (2016) 'Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for the conterminous United States, early 1990s' 30 m raster, as aggregated to NHDPlusV2 in ScienceBase item 58d9dec6e4b0543bf7fda70e (CAT_TILES_Early90s), is largely MISSING over this project's basins. Verified by direct computation: 25.6% of the sensor basins have area-weighted CAT_NODATA of exactly 100% (i.e. no source coverage at all), and 42.7% have CAT_NODATA above 50%; the median area-weighted NODATA across basins is 95.84% and the mean is 74.35%. Nationally, 2,689,897 of 2,699,864 COMIDs carry a value but only 12.1% are greater than zero and the national mean is 2.392%. THE CRITICAL TRAP: this layer reports 0.0 rather than null where the source grid is absent, so every basin at the bottom of the sorted list (USGS-415959091441301, WQS0111, WQS0025, WQS0022, WQS0063) has tile percent 0.0 paired with NODATA 100% — a naive ingest would encode 'no data' as 'no tile drainage' and inject a systematic, spatially structured false signal into exactly the between-site term the project is trying to fix. Where both layers have data the two tile products correlate only r=0.688, so they are not interchangeable. Recommendation: use CAT_TILES92/TOT_TILES92 (complete coverage, see companion claim) and always read the paired NODATA column, masking values where NODATA exceeds a threshold. This is the concrete resolution of the project's open 'tile drainage: no data source identified' item — a source exists, is free and CC0, but the obvious 30 m candidate is the wrong one for Iowa.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 25.6% of basins have 100% NODATA; 42.7% have >50% NODATA; median area-weighted NODATA 95.84%; nationally only 12.1% of COMIDs >0, mean 2.392%; correlation with TILES92 only r=0.688

tier3_unverified.claim: THE MANURE-VERSUS-COMMERCIAL NITROGEN SPLIT IS AVAILABLE AT COMID, BUT FOR 2012 ONLY. ScienceBase item 59038bc8e4b0e862d2311aef ('Select Chemical Attributes: Nitrogen and Phosphorous Estimates from Fertilizer and Manure, 2012') ships eight separate zipped CSVs whose field definitions were verified from the FGDC metadata XML: FarmN2012/FarmP2012 = commercial fertilizer applied on agricultural land (source: Brakebill and others, USGS 2017, 'County-Level Estimates of Nitrogen and Phosphorus from Commercial Fertilizer for the Conterminous United States, 1987-2012'); TN2012/TP2012 = nutrients from MANURE on agricultural land (source: Gronberg and others, USGS 2017, 'County-level estimates of nitrogen and phosphorus from animal manure (2007 and 2012)'); RCFN2012/RCFP2012 and RCTN2012/RCTP2012 = the same fertilizer and manure quantities restricted to ROW CROP land specifically. Units are kilograms, with -9999 as NODATA, and each ships CAT_/ACC_/TOT_ plus NODATA columns. This directly supplies the requested manure-vs-commercial decomposition and a row-crop-weighted variant, at basin-aggregatable resolution, CC0, no authentication. HOWEVER IT DOES NOT SOLVE THE POST-2017 CLIFF: this is a single 2012 snapshot, not a time series, and the underlying Brakebill fertilizer series itself ends in 2012 — five years EARLIER than the gTREND surplus product that already ends in 2017. Its correct use is therefore precisely the static-basin-attribute framing: one scalar per basin encoding that basin's relative N-input rank, which is a different and untested construct from the failed experiment of broadcasting 2017 surplus forward as a time-varying feature (that experiment scored -0.166 and does NOT falsify static-rank use). The falsifiable test is whether a basin's N-input rank is stable enough over 2008-2026 that a 2012 snapshot carries between-site signal.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 8 CSVs; fields FarmN2012 (commercial fertilizer), TN2012 (manure), RCFN2012 (fertilizer on row crop), RCTN2012 (manure on row crop); units kg; single year 2012 only

tier3_unverified.claim: THE SUBSURFACE-RESIDENCE-TIME AND SOIL-DRAINAGE ATTRIBUTES ON THE PROJECT'S WISHLIST ALL EXIST AS COMID-JOINABLE STATIC TABLES IN THIS SAME CC0 RELEASE, each with CAT_/ACC_/TOT_ and NODATA columns, each downloadable as a zipped CSV over unauthenticated HTTPS, each covering full CONUS including out-of-state basin area. Verified by fetching each item's metadata: (a) CONTACT TIME — 'the length of time it takes for water to drain along subsurface flow paths to the stream', units DAYS, computed from basin topography, soil porosity and soil hydraulic conductivity, source Wolock (USGS, written commun. 2014) per methods of Wolock and others (1997), item 56f96fc5e4b0a6037df06b12 — this is the requested subsurface residence/transit-time proxy; (b) BASE FLOW INDEX — ratio of base flow to total flow as a PERCENT, source Wolock (2003) 'Base-flow index grid for the conterminous United States', item 5669a8e3e4b08895842a1d4f; (c) AVERAGE ELEVATION OF WATER TABLE RELATIVE TO LAND SURFACE — units METERS below land surface, source Ying Fan and others (Rutgers, written commun. 2007), item 56f97456e4b0a6037df06b50; (d) ESTIMATED MEAN ANNUAL NATURAL GROUNDWATER RECHARGE — units mm/yr, 30-year 1951-1980 mean, source Wolock (2003), item 56f97577e4b0a6037df06b5a; (e) TOPOGRAPHIC WETNESS INDEX ln(a/tan(beta)), source Wolock and McCabe (1995), item 56f97be4e4b0a6037df06b70; (f) STATSGO2 HYDROLOGIC GROUPS — percent of catchment in each hydrologic soil group (USDA 2010), item 5728d93be4b0b13d3918a99f; (g) SSURGO SOIL RESTRICTIVE LAYER — estimated percent presence of a restrictive layer in the upper 25, 35, 45 and 55 cm of agricultural land, source Nakagaki and others (2012), item 572900afe4b0b13d3918aa64. Additional relevant items in the same release include riparian-buffer NLCD (50 m and 100 m buffer versions, items 57855ddee4b0e02680bf37bf and 64959e63d34ef77fcb01dcb7), percent watershed covered by waterbodies (57ab4009e4b05e859be1ad26), and mean flow-path distance to streams (5d1a1dfbe4b0941bde6025d2). NO EFFECT SIZES ON NITRATE ARE REPORTED IN THIS DATA RELEASE — it is a data product, not a study, so it establishes availability and operational feasibility only, and every one of these must be tested empirically under the project's LOFO protocol. FLAG THE n=19 CONSTRAINT: this release makes dozens of static basin attributes trivially available, which creates a severe overfitting hazard when the between-site regression has roughly 19 independent units — attributes should be added in a small preselected set with LOFO evaluation, not swept in bulk.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 7 wishlist attributes confirmed available with units and sources; no nitrate effect sizes reported (data release, not a study)

tier3_unverified.claim: AgTile-US is a STATIC single-year product representing 2017 only. Its inputs are USDA Census of Agriculture 2017 county-level tile-drainage acreage, SSURGO v2.0 soil drainage class (7 categories, excessively drained through very poorly drained), SRTM-derived 30-m topographic slope, and the NLCD 2016 'cultivated cropland' mask. There is no time series and no annual update in this release, so it can only be used as a static basin attribute, not as a time-varying feature. tier3_unverified.claim: The AgTile-US spatial pattern is NOT independently observed — it is a downscaling of county Census totals. The algorithm iterates within each county: start with the most poorly drained SSURGO class (D=7) at 0% slope, increase slope in 1% steps until accumulated area reaches the county Census target, and on hitting a 20% slope ceiling drop to the next drainage class (D=6) and reset slope to 0%, then fine-tune in 0.1% increments to minimize absolute error against the county total. Consequence for this project: a basin-aggregated tile fraction from AgTile-US is essentially a deterministic function of (county Census tile acreage, SSURGO drainage class, slope) and is therefore substantially COLLINEAR with any separately added SSURGO hydrologic-soil-group or slope feature. Falsifiable: reproduce the R code at github.com/NCAR/AgTile-US and confirm no observational tile-location data enters the model.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 20% upper slope threshold; 1% coarse then 0.1% fine slope increments; 7 SSURGO drainage classes

IOWA SPECIFICALLY: 91.1% accuracy on 5,253 ground-truth points. This is a map-accuracy validation, not a predictive-model split, so no spatial-holdout comparison to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820 is possible or meaningful. tier3_unverified.claim: AgTile-US estimates 22,340,442 ha of tile-drained cropland for CONUS, of which Iowa is 5,706,831 ha — the largest of any state — followed by Illinois 3,836,371 ha, Minnesota 3,264,744 ha, Indiana 2,572,162 ha and Ohio 2,178,405 ha. Agreement with the USDA Census county totals it was calibrated to is −0.35% CONUS-wide and better than −0.25% for the heavily tile-drained Midwestern states (this closeness is expected by construction, since the county totals are the calibration target, and is therefore NOT independent evidence of accuracy). Falsifiable: check the per-state area table and the Census-comparison figure.

Stated AgTile-US error sources that bound how much signal a basin-level tile fraction can carry: the NLCD 2016 cultivated-cropland mask underrepresents cropland by 18% CONUS-wide (up to 92% in West Virginia); the USDA Census itself carries an average error margin of 19.8%; accuracy falls monotonically with increasing slope and with better-drained soil classes, exceeding 98% only in very poorly/poorly drained soils at ≤1% slope; worst state-level biases are New Mexico −79.06%, West Virginia −42.38%, Mississippi −15.90%, Texas −11.53%; and substituting a coarser 90-m DEM costs about 2% accuracy. For flat, poorly drained Iowa basins the product sits in its best-performing regime, but roughly 20% Census-level uncertainty in the county totals propagates directly into any basin aggregate. Falsifiable: check the Usage Notes / limitations section for each figure.

tier3_unverified.claim: The 2017 farm-fertilizer values in Falcone (2021) are MODEL OUTPUT, not measurements, and this matters for treating 2017 differently from 1950-2012. AAPFCO state-level fertilizer tonnage for 2017 was never completed (report cites J. Slater, University of Missouri, written commun., May 4, 2020: the AAPFCO 2017 data 'have not been completed', and 'no other State-level summaries of fertilizer use by weight' were available), so Falcone substituted a random-forest regression with 11 predictors (percent county area in corn, pasture, N-fixing, small-grain, misc crops; fertilizer dollars divided by fertilizer-price index; manure N or P kg; annual ET; annual precipitation; fertilized acres; population density), trained on 9,198 records (3,066 counties x years 2002, 2007, 2012) with published county masses from Brakebill & Gronberg (2017) as the target, 1,000 trees. Reported out-of-bag proportion of variance explained: r2 = 0.948 for the nitrogen model and r2 = 0.921 for the phosphorus model. Dominant predictor by a wide margin: county fertilizer expenditure in dollars (%IncMSE 73.3 for N, 67.7 for P), next fertilized acres (34.9 / 28.3), then pasture percent (24.7 / 26.7), population density (22.4 / 20.4), ET and PPT (22.1 / 20.8 each), corn percent (23.0 / 22.5), N-fixing percent (20.7 / 27.6), misc crops (19.3 / 18.7), small grain (15.4 / 13.3), manure kg (15.9 / 13.9). CAUTION: the r2 = 0.948 is an OOB estimate over a random-ish resample of county-years, NOT a spatially held-out estimate, so it is not directly comparable to any leave-one-basin-out number and likely overstates transfer to unseen counties.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: RF OOB variance explained r2 = 0.948 (N), 0.921 (P); n_train = 9,198 county-years; 11 predictors; 1,000 trees; top predictor %IncMSE 73.3
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (3,066 counties x 3 years = 9,198 county-year records; no basins)

tier3_unverified.claim: The Falcone manure series can be extended past the 2017 cliff without any new data product, because the manure method needs only (a) county livestock inventories from USDA NASS QuickStats and (b) published fixed coefficients. Falcone's stated procedure: multiply county head counts (beef cows, milk cows, other cattle, hogs, broilers, layers, turkeys, sheep, horses) by the nutrient-production formulas of Gronberg & Arnold (2017), then by a livestock-weight coefficient equal to average federally-inspected live slaughter weight in the target year divided by that in the 1992 base year. The published 2017 coefficients are cattle 1.152, hogs 1.117, sheep 1.078, broilers 1.374, chickens 1.295, turkeys 1.425 (horses held static because USDA reports no weight). Since the 2022 Census of Agriculture is published and this repo already contains experiments/erin/data/NASSAgCensusDownload2022.xlsx and experiments/erin/create_county_data_2022.ipynb, a 2022 manure-N county layer is reproducible with existing assets. FALSIFIABLE AND FAILURE MODE: USDA withholds county values for disclosure. Falcone reports that withheld hog counties grew from 26 (1974) to 212 (1992) to 576 (2012), and for 2017 he backfilled 515 withheld hog counties from the most recent prior year (up to 6 census periods / 30 years back), leaving only 14 unfillable. So a 2022 extension inherits a growing imputation burden concentrated exactly in counties with one very large confinement operation - i.e. the high-manure counties that matter most for Iowa nitrate.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 2017 weight coefficients: cattle 1.152, hogs 1.117, broilers 1.374, chickens 1.295, turkeys 1.425, sheep 1.078. Withheld hog counties: 26 (1974) -> 212 (1992) -> 576 (2012) -> 515 backfilled in 2017, 14 left blank

tier3_unverified.claim: A CATCHMENT-LEVEL (not county-level) successor product exists and is a better fit for this project's pipeline than Falcone's county tables: Sekellick, A.J., and Sherr, C.E., 2024, 'Nitrogen and phosphorus inputs from fertilizer and manure in the Continental United States, 2002-2017', USGS data release DOI 10.5066/P9WDBIXC, published 26 September 2024. It downscales the county-level estimates to NHDPlus Version 2.1 catchments keyed by COMID using NLCD land-cover classes, for the years 2002, 2007, 2012, and 2017. Eight CSV tables covering total N and total P from four source categories: agricultural fertilizer, confined animal manure, unconfined animal manure, and developed-land fertilizer. CONUS coverage (so multi-state basins are complete). Format CSV plus XML metadata; license CC0 1.0 Universal; bulk download, no authentication. OPERATIONAL RELEVANCE: this project already stores an NHDPlus COMID per basin and delineates arbitrary map pins via USGS NLDI (which returns COMIDs), so these tables join by COMID with NO county-to-basin areal reapportionment step and NO dependence on any observation at the target site - it satisfies the ungauged-arbitrary-pin deployment constraint. The confined-vs-unconfined manure split is additional information that neither the county Falcone tables nor the gTREND surplus product provides. CAVEAT: it still ends at 2017; it does not solve the post-2017 cliff, only the spatial-aggregation and multi-state-truncation problems.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: NHDPlusV2.1 catchment resolution (COMID-keyed); 4 years (2002, 2007, 2012, 2017); 8 tables; 4 source categories x N and P; CONUS
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (CONUS NHDPlusV2 catchments, ~2.6 million nationally; no model performance reported)
